BY WIRE.
Dr. Joseph Pancoast, emeritus professor of anatomy at Jefferson college, Philadelphia, died the morning, aged 77, after a short illness of pneumonia.

Mrs. Harriet Bell, a respectable tailoress, was fatally stabbed on Kirkland street, Boston, about 8 o'clock this morning by a man whoni a few minutes before she died she declared she did not know. The murderer escaped.

The funeral of the late Judge Lathrop, receiver and president of the Central railroad of New Jersey, took place to-day and was largely attended by prominent railroad officials.

"Mysterious flames" last night caused a $40,000 loss in Oberlin, O., including Rowlands & Brokson's drug store which the temperance people have been seeking to close up because of the spirituous liquors alleged to be sold there.

J. N. Dubarry was to-day elected president of the Southwest Pennsylvania railroad, a branch of the Pennsylvania.

The accused Philadelphia star routers have renewed their bail for appearance at the May term of the United States court.

Theison's furniture warcrooms at Canton, N. Y., burned to-day. Loss $20,000, partially insured.

There was a timely discovery of an attempt to wreck a passenger train on the Illinois Midland railroad, near Decatur, Ill., last night.

More Nihilists have been arrested at Odessa and further plots discovered.

Largen beat Gookin by two lengths in the boat race on the Thames championship course to-day.

Gen. Bingham's resolution granting the use of arms, tents and equipments to the G. A. R. for their encampment on the Gettysburg battle field next July, passed the House to-day.
Mr. Beecher, whose sudden illness last night is supposed to have been caused by the bad water of Chicago, is much better and left there at noon to-day for Rock Island, where he will lecture to-night.
Hamilton Howe, an undertaker, was instantly killed and ten others were seriously wounded by the fall of a wall at a fire in Strathroy, Out., to day.
Masked men attacked the jail at Del Norte, Col., and riddled with bullets Arnold Howe and Frank Young, confined there on a charge of stealing cattle. Bob Sawyer, a negro, was lynched at Franklin, Ky., for an attempted assault on a white girl.
The New Jersey Central railroad depot, at Valley Station, about ten miles from Easton, was with its contents entirely destroyed by fire at 5 o'clock this morning, by a spark from the locomotive.
Work was generally suspended to-day at all the mines of the Lehigh & Wilkes-barre coal company, on account of the funeral of F. S. Lathrop, late president of that company.
The United States grand jury at New York to-day brought an indictment against General N. M. Curtis, special treasury agent, for having collected money from government employees to defray the expenses of the Republican state committee.
Two buildings connected with the American powder company at Acton, five miles northwest of Sudbury, Mass., exploded at twenty minutes past 9 o'clock this morning with a terrific crash. The particulars of the disaster have not been received as yet.

In the United States court at Trenton, this morning, Henry B. Marshbank, who pleaded guilty on five indictments for embezzlement and conspiracy to defraud the First national bank of Newark, was sentenced to five years imprisonment in the state prison. Edward White, a letter carrier of New Brunswick, N. J., was sentenced to pay a fine of $250 for purloining letters.

Mrs. Peter Goodhart was run over and instantly killed by a coal train at Reading to-day.

Good authority says that the President yesterday tendered to Senator Edmunds the position of Associate Justice of the Supreme Court, and that Senator Edmunds declined it.

The anthracite coal interests have agreed to the stoppage of coal mining on the 9th, 10th, 11th, 16th, 27th, 18th, 23d, 24th and 25th of this month.

A Jail Attacked and Prisoners Shot.
DENVER (Col.) March 6th —The Republic.
A Jail Attacked and Prisoners Shot.
DENVER (Col.), March 6th. — The Republican's special says: Arnold Howard and Frank Young, charged with cattle-stealing, were arrested Thursday and placed in jail at Del Norte. The next day an attempt was made to break jail, but was prevented. Saturday night 100 mounted man, said to be stock men from the Rio Grande and San Luis valleys, rode down on the guards, ordered them to throw up their hand and commenced firing in every direction. When the jail was broken the prisoners attempted to escape. Young was mortally wounded and Howard was killed outright. The body of the latter was thrown into the river. The windows of the jail were riddled with bullets. Howard has been arrested twelve times on a charge of cattle stealing, and in every instance was cleared.

Municipal Elections.
PORTLAND (Me.), March 6th. — The vote for Mayor of the city resulted in no choice. Libby (Rep.) 2,719; Deering (Citizens' and Democrat.) 2,259; Littlefield (Temperance), 483; scattering, 47. The Republicans elect all the School Committees, five Aldermen and fourteen Councilmen. The Democrats elect one Alderman and six Councilmen. No election for one Alderman and one Councilman.

Hollowell elects James H. Leigh (Rep.) Mayor by 252 majority; also the straight Republican ticket in every ward. This result has not been attained in that city for many years.

David Farrar (Rep.) is elected Mayor of Lewiston over Garcelon (Fusion) by a vote of 1,348 to 900. The Republicans elect five Aldermen and the Democrats elect two. In Auburn Gao, S. Woodman (Rep.) is elected Mayor by a small majority.

MOBILE (Ala.), March 6th. — At the municipal election to-day the straight Democratic ticket was successful—electing the Mayor, Municipal Board and probably Tax Collector.

Supreme Court Decisions.
WASHINGTON, March 6th. — Among the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court to-day were the following:

John L. Heald, plaintiff in error, vs. Harver W. Rice, in error to the Circuit Court of the United States for the District of California—Judgment reversed with costs, and cause remanded for trial. Opinion by Gray.

B. Poppe, plaintiff in error, vs. B. T. Langford, in error to the Supreme Court of California—Dismissed for want of jurisdiction. Opinion by Chief Justice.

Hanged Himself in Jail.

MARQUETTE (Mich.). March 6th.—Mike Dwyer, in jail, hanged himself to-day. He was a resident of Montreal.

Reform at Chicago.

CHICAGO, March 6th.—Some sixty of the arrested gamblers gave bonds to-day in $250 each to appear for an early trial.

The clergy are moving unitedly to stop Sunday theatrical performances, and will exhaust every method to accomplish that end.

Destruction by Fire.

BALTIMORE, March 6th.—Prince Frederick, the county seat of Calvert county, was almost destroyed by fire to-day. Loss, $50,000; insurance slight.

A Berder Affair Which Results Fa- tally to a Couple of Officers.
Del Norte Vigilantes Make Short Work of Cattle Thieves.
To-day's Crime Record.

To-day's Crime Record.
A KENTUCKY AFFAIR.

Nashville, March 7—Bob Carver (colored) was lynched at Franklyn, Ky., last night for an attempt to rape a white girl 16 years old named Reilly.

CATTLE THIEVES LYNCHED.

Denver, March 7—On Thursday last Arnold Howard and Frank Young, charged with stealing cattle, were arrested and placed in jail at Del Norte. The next day an attempt was made to break the jail, but was prevented. Saturday night a hundred mounted men, said to be stock men from the Rio Grande and San Louis valleys rode down on the guards, ordered them to throw up their hands and commenced firing in every direction. When the jail was broken open the prisoners attempted to escape. Young was mortally wounded and Howard was killed outright. The body of the latter was thrown into the river. The windows of the jail were riddled with bullets. Howard has been arrested twelve times charged with cattle stealing and in every instance was cleared.

WHISKEY THE CAUSE OF IT.

St. Louis, March 7.—Santa Fe special: Governor Sheldon received news from Toos Pueblo yesterday, which substantiated is serious. It is to the effect that four days ago some Toos Pueblos became drunk. They were arrested and placed in jail. They escaped and deputy Sheriff Myers and Martinez started to Pueblo to re-arrest them. They and their posse were met by fifty-nine armed Pueblo Indians and a fight ensued, in which Deputy Sheriff Myers was killed and Deputy Sheriff Martinez mortally wounded. The murderers are not yet captured. The Toos Pueblos is one of the richest and largest tribes in the territory and heretofore the best of feeling has existed between the Pueblos and the surrounding Mexican towns. Of late too much whiskey traffic has been going on, which the United States authorities should stop. Gov. Sheldon has sent to Toos for latest information and the news is hourly expected.

FATAL AFFRAY.

Arkadelphia, Ark., March 7—In a shooting affray yesterday one negro was killed and two mortally hurt.

CIVIL SERVICE REFORM.

New York, March 7—The grand jury has indicted Special Treasury Agent Curtis for asking for money for political purposes.

MANGLED REMAINS.

Terra Haute, March 7—The mangled remains of a woman have been found along the railroad track near the city. Evidence of foul play has been discovered.

MURDER WITHOUT CAUSE.

Boston, March 7—An unknown man this morning cut the throat of Harriett Ball, while walking near her home. The assassin escaped. No cause known. She died in two minutes.

MISCELLANEOUS.
A QUARRELSOME drunkard named John Davidson killed his aged mother, in Philadelphia, Pa., May 4. There had been an altercation over some money matters, during which pans and chairs were thrown about the rooms, and John seized a hatchet and struck his mother a savage blow on the top of the head. This he repeated time after time, until the woman's brains were scattered on the floor, when the neighbors, startled by the tumult, rushed in.

PROHIBITION is enforced with dynamite in Cedarville, Ohio. One end of C. Sweeney's saloon, near the railway, was blown out on the 4th, the owner, his wife, and children being thrown from bed to the floor. An attempt was made to destroy Caldwell's drug store, but the charge did not explode.

Mrs. Newton, of Louisville, Ky., apprehensive that the father of her adopted son would take him from her, gave the little fellow a dose of morphine, on the 3d, wrote a note of explanation, and then drugged herself. The boy died. Mrs. Newton will probably recover.

DE LONG and eleven men have been found by Engineer Melville. They were all dead.

Thurmond, at Dallas, Texas, rendered a verdict of guilty of manslaughter, and Cowart was sentenced to the Penitentiary for seven years. A motion for a new trial was granted on the ground that the verdict was not in accordance with the evidence.

geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A1:
HORRIBLE MURDER.
Arrest and Confession of the Murderers.
Advices from Ashland, Ky., state that the murderers of the Gibbons children have been arrested on the confesssion of one of them. All live in Ashland, and two of them are married men. They are in the Cattleburg jail. Lynching is expected tonight.

A special from Ashland, Ky.. says: The three men arrested for the Gibbons murder are Wm. Neal, Ellis Craft and Geo. Ellis, all white. Ellis says Craft and Neal awakened him on the night of the murder and urged him to go with them to the Gibbons house. He went reluctantly. They entered by a window, and Neal and Craft outraged the two girls. Emma Thomas recognized Neal and said she would tell her mother. Robert, the boy, was then about to give an alarm when Craft struck him on the head with an axe, killing him instantly. Craft then told Fanny her time to die had come, and amid viteous cries of the child for mercy, he struck her on the head and killed her instantly. Neal then killed Emma Thomas in the same way. Craft and Neal at first denied Ellis' story, but Neal confessed this afternoon and both he and Ellis waived an examination. Craft will have a hearing Thursday. Ellis and Neal are married; Craft is single. They were all present when Gibbon's residence was burned and one of them drove the hearse at the funeral and another was a pall bearer. Crowds have been gathering all day at Cattlesburg and threats of lynching are common.

THE ASHLAND AFFAIR. Mason County Guards Ordered to Catlettsburg to Protect the Murderers From Mob Violence.
The following despatch from Adjutant General J. P. Nuckols, was received last night at 10 o'clock by Capt. A. C. Respess, of the Mason County Guards:

FRANKF RT, KY., January 4, 1882.

Captain A. C. Repess, or Lieut. Dressell, commanding Mason County Guards: Special order No. 1.—Capt. A. C. Respess or the officer in command of the Mason County Guards, Maysville, will proceed with his company by the first steamer to Catlettsburg, on the Big Sandy River, and he will, on arrival at Catlettsburg, report to the Hon. G. M. Brown, Judge of the 16th Judicial District, and carry out his orders in maintaining the public peace. Vouchers for transportation will be paid on presentation out of the treasury. It is of the utmost importance that the company proceed to night and the entire strength of the company is desired to go. Capt. Respess or the ranking officer present, must not fail to act promptly in the execution of this order. Advise me at what moment you can leave. Take twenty rounds of ammunition. By order of Governor Blackburn. J. P. Nuckols, Adjt. Gen.

THE WEST.
Kentucky.
Determined Vigilantes—A Sheriff's Race for Life With His Prisoners.

CATLETTSBUG, Jan. 5.—The three men who murdered two girls after outraging them and also murdered a brother of one of the girls to prevent him raising an alarm, afterwards firing the house, during the absence of the father of two of the victims, Mr. Gibson, at Ashland, were secretly moved from jail by the sheriff this afternoon to save them from being lynched by the crowd that had organized for the purpose. The sheriff took the prisoners in a close cab aboard a ferryboat bound for Ohio. The vigilantes learning of this chartered the steamboat Mountain Girl and boarding her went in pursuit. The sheriff, when he learned that he was pursued, headed for down the river and at last accounts it was a race for life.

geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A10:
THE ASHLAND FIENDS.
A Narrow Escape from the Hands of the Mob.
The Scoundrels Placed on a Steamboat and Started for Maysville-The Mob Take Possession of Another and Pursue.
A LONG AND EXCITING CHASE.
First Dispatch.
sarmo Ky. January 5.
First Dispatch.

CATLETTSBURG, Ky., January 5.—A special says: Judge Brown, fearing the great crowd from Ashland would prevent the hearing of the cases of the Gibbons family murders, ordered the steamer Mountain Girl to get up steam and take the prisoners to Maysville, Ky., for safe keeping. Owing to the difficulty of getting the prisoners on board the sheriff put them on the ferry boat and started down the river. The mob took possession of the steamer Mountain Girl, and started in pursuit. It is thought that the prisoners will not get to Maysville alive.

Second Dispatch.

IRONTON, Ohio. January 5.—The trial at Catlettsburg, of the Ashland murderers, was set for 1 o'clock. Judge Brown, fearing the action of the mob, about 2,000 strong, had the prisoners placed on a ferry boat which transferred them to the Mountain Boy, at the Sheridan's coal works, three miles below Catlettsburg. The mob hearing this, captured the steamer Mountain Girl, and are in hot pursuit. Mountain Boy passed here, ten miles from Catlettsburg, with prisoners, at 2 P. M., the Mountain Girl not here yet.

2:40 P. M.—It is supposed that Mountain Boy will be overtaken before she reaches Maysville, as the Mountain Girl stopped at Ashland, and the mob are now making efforts to secure a train to head off the Mountain Boy at Portsmouth or the nearest port below.

Another Account.

CINCINNATI, January 5.—The Gazette's Ashland, Ky., special says: Judge Brown, upon hearing that a mob was coming from Ashland to lynch the prisoners, issued an order for the removal of the prisoners to the Mason county (Maysville) jail, and Craft having waived an examination he adjourned the Circuit Court till January 16th.

Citizens here are very indignant at Brown. They had gone to protect the prisoners, and the prosecuting committee had asked the Governor for troops to assist in keeping order, and it was in response to this that the troops were started up from Maysville. The citizens sent a committee to Judge Brown to ask him to rescind his order, but he refused.

A dispatch has been sent Senator Moore to get an act passed, to-morrow, appointing a session of the court next Monday for the trial.

VANCEBURG, Ky., January 5.—The steamer Mountain Boy arrived here at 7:30 with the Ashland fiends on board, expecting to reach their destination, the Maysville jail, about midnight.

Sheriff John Kounz left Greenup at six o'clock and embarked on the B. F. Enos for Catlettsburg, arriving there at 10:30, in time to attend the preliminary examination of Ellis Craft. Craft waived an examination.

The excitement was rife, and the rapidly growing crowd threatened violence. Word was received that a train, loaded with lynchers, had started from Ashland, and was expected at any time. Fearing the mob, the Mountain Girl, which was lying at the wharf, was chartered to convey the prisoners to Maysville.

While the Girl was raising steam, the train from Ashland rolled in, with about 500 determined regulators on board. The Sheriff, with a party of ten guards, by an adroit movement, removed the prisoners from the jail to the wharf.

As soon as the crowd beheld the prisoners, they started down the bank with loud yells of indignation, gathering arms and missles ready for an assault. The Sheriff, seeing the mob descending, and the Girl not yet having steam up, boarded the ferry boat with his party, and turned her down stream. The mob took possession of the Mountain Girl, cut her loose and commenced a determined chase.

The Mountain Girl not having sufficient steam pressure, soon fell behind, but in a short time she got in shape and commenced gaining rapidly on the slow ferry, and in a short time the Girl approached so closely that a capture seemed imminent, but fortunately the Mountain Boy, a faster boat than the Girl, approached on the scene, on her regular trip up from Ashland to Louisiana, She was hailed by the Sheriff and pressed into service, and the party rapidly transferred to her. When the transfer had been successfully made, the girl Black with an excited, enraged and howling mob, was right on their heels, and the exciting chase was resumed. But the Boy, flying light, showed her a clean pair of heels.

Near Ashland, the Hudson with the Kentucky militia, was met in mid stream. Capt. A. C. Respess, of the Mason County Guards and twenty-five men were transferred to the Boy and took charge of the prisoners. The pursuing vessel was still in sight, but when they learned was commenced a determined chase.

MAYSVILLE. January 5.—The Ashland murderers arrived here at 10 o'clock tonight, and were safely lodged in jail.

Owing to an accident to the Scotia the Katie Stockdale did not leave on her regular trip Thursday, but laid over until next Monday to take the Scotia's day.

Arrival of the Ashland Prisoners at Maysville.

Capt. A. C. Respess, with a detachment of the Mason County Guards, who left here yesterday morning for Catlettsburg, in obedience to orders from the Governor, arrived here last night, at ten o'clock by the steamer Mountain Boy, having in custody Neal, Craft and Ellis, the men arrested on the charge of having committed the recent horrible murder at Ashland, Ky. Yesterday morning, at Catlettsburg, a mob numbering probably two thousand persons, collected for the avowed purpose of lynching the prisoners, but the sheriff and posse under pretense of arraigning them for their preliminary examination, took them to the court house, and subsequently removed them by a back door to the river where the Mountain Girl was supposed to be in readiness to take them sway, but when the sheriff reached the boat it was found to have only 20 pounds of steam. They were then taken to a a ferryboat, closely followed by the mob, but reached it in advance of them and succeeded in getting away from the landing. The mob seized the Mountain Girl and raising steam by the use of rosin followed in pursuit. Several miles below Catlettsburg the sheriff's party met the Mountain Boy
coming up and transfering the prisoners to her she was turned about and headed down stream, the Mountain Girl still following. Near Riverton the Hudson was met, having the guards on board. They were transferred to the Mountain Boy and the pursuit here ended. The prisoners on their arrival at this place were placed in the jail, which has since been closely guarded by the troops. Capt. Respess, in obedience to orders from Judge George N. Brown, of the sixteenth district, will take the prisoners to Catlettsburg for trial on the 16th inst. The services of the soldiery will probably be needed until the trial is over.

The prisoners are bad looking men and of a brutal type. Neal is about thirty years of age and has been a mill hand at the Northern Iron Works, at Ashland. Craft, who is about the same age, is a farmer by occupation and is considered the shrewdest of the three. Ellis is probably thirty-three years of age and is a laborer. He has confessed to participating in the murder, and claims to have been forced to take the part he did. He has admitted that the Gibbons and Thomas girls were ravished, and that he and his companions were guilty alike. He says also, that he poured coal oil upon the bodies of the girls and the crippled boy preparatory to burning the house. On the way down the river Craft and Neal manifested a stolid indifference to their situation. Ellis, especially while the mob was present exhibited the most object terror. Neal and Craft both claim to be innocent and assert their ability to prove an alibi, at the proper time.

The jail here it is well-known is in such a condition that the safe keeping of prisoners, cannot be assured. It is necessary
a constant guard should be maintained, which the County Judge has ordered to be done.
geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A12: punishing criminals in Kentucky which, though not strictly in accordance with the law, saves the State many trials and the expenses attached to them. The latest news states that the Governor of Kentucky in order to save the murderers of the Gibbons family from being lynched put them on a ferry boat and started down the river with them to lodge them in Maysville jail, while the mob had seized the steamer Mountain Girl, and started after them in hot pursuit.
geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A13:
THE ASHLAND MURDERERS.
Taken Down the Ohio River in a Steamer Parsued by a Mob.
Yesterday a mob of 450 men started from Ashland, Ky., to go to Cattlettsburgh, some five miles off, for the purpose of lynching Neal, Ellis and Craft, the murderers of Annie Thomas and the Gibbons children. Judge Bowen, becoming uneasy, ordered the prisoners to be taken on board the steamer Mountain Boy, and to be taken to Maysville, from which place a company of soldiers had been ordered.

The sheriff took the prisoners and with difficulty got them on the steamer. Just as she started away the Ashland mob took possession of the steamer Mountain Girl and started in pursuit. At Riverton, about twenty miles below Cattlettsburgh, the steamer Mountain Boy was met by steamer Hudson, which had on board the Maysville guards, numbering 75 muskets. The soldiers were transferred to the Mountain Boy, which then continued down the river, passing Portsmouth at about 5½ p.m. Those on the Mountain Girl, on learning that the murderers were in the care of the militia, wisely gave up the pursuit, and, turning around, started for home. The chase created the greatest excitement all along the river towns, and when the Mountain Boy landed at Portsmouth for coal it was all the troops could do to prevent the people from boarding the steamer at all hazards. It is expected that the prisoners will be safely lodged in Maysville jail soon after midnight.

At Cattlettsburgh there were threats of lynching Judge Strong for sending the prisoners away, and he and Judge Savage kept closely within doors.

A special from Ashland says that the men went to Cattlettsburgh to protect the prisoners and see that they had a fair trial.

Judge Brown had notice of their intention, and hence the bitterest feeling exists against him for sending the prisoners away.

An indignation meeting was held and a resolution adopted, declaring their intention to bring back the prisoners, and pledging their honor to protect them until they have had a fair trial.

A committee was also appointed to wait on Judge Brown and induce him to rescind his order, but the judge refused to do so.

At a later hour a mass meeting was held, and a resolution adopted to appeal to the Legislature for a court to be held on next Monday for the trial of the prisoners. The excitement over the case is intense.
geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A23:
THE ASHLAND MURDERERS.
Their Approaching Trial-The People Satisfied for the Law to Take Its Course.
CINCINNATI, January 9.—A Catlettsburg, Ky., special says: "The grand jury was impanelled to-day under the special act of the Kentucky Legislature, convening the court to try the Ashland murderers. The foreman of the jury is John Russell, of Ashland, one of the Citizens' Committee formed to arrest and prosecute the perpetrators of this triple crime. The jury is said to be the best ever gathered in Boyd county. It is supposed that they will not report till Tuesday morning. The prisoners, under a guard of State troops, arrive on Wednesday morning. The feeling is that so long as the law takes its regular course towards a speedy trial there will be no danger of interference by the people, but if another attempt is made to remove the prisoners it will be hard to restrain the fury of the people."

MR. CANNON, the delegate in Congress from Utah, is not strengthening his position by his charges that the ministers of the gospel over the country are endeavoring to shape public sentiment against polygamous practices. He will find, if he looks a little closer into the matter, that a very considerable majority of the people of the United States who are not preachers are decidedly opposed to and in favor of legally suppressing polygamy. Public sentiment is already molded on that subject.

When the late horrible murder was committed at Ashland, a mob, one of the largest that ever gathered in the state, endeavored to lynch the perpetrators, but the strong arm of the law interfered and they were removed from the impending danger. A special term of the court to try them was authorized by the Legislature, and in very little over thirty days from the time the crime was committed, two of the murderers have been tried, convicted, and sentenced to death. Can any state in the union show prompter and more efficient administration of the law?

A WEATHER prophet enlivening New Jersey with his presence, predicts that the present month will be characterized by heavy snows, severe cold and very high winds. He says the change will take place this week and after that time and during the month the wind will be high, and ladies are warned to take a reef in their skirts and a few inches, off the brims of their Gainsboroughs. The railroads will be blockaded, rubber boots will be in demand, but skating will not be good. Snows will be especially deep in the Ohio Valley. Coal dealers should hasten along their supplies, for the river will be frozen up so tight the steamboating will be suspended until late in the spring.

LAW AND LYNCHERS.
Murder, Suicide and Retribution.
Dr. Joseph A. Begs, bookkeeper a
Murder, Suicide and Retribution.

Dr. Joseph A. Beggs, bookkeeper and chemist at the Alice furnace, Ironton, Ohio, was cruelly murdered on Wednesday night about 8 o'clock a short distance above the city. The murderers used a shotgun, loaded with buckshot and slugs. John Wagner and Bill Seek have been arrested as the murderers. Wagner confessed firing two shots at Beggs, but says it was in self-defense. Beggs bore a high character.

About three o'clock yesterday morning a party of masked men, numbering 75 or 100, took from the jail at Oxford, Granville county, N. C., John Brodie and Shadrack Hester, colored, charged with the murder of T. M. Lynch, and hanged them in a grove of trees near the spot where the murder was committed. To get at the prisoners the jailer was taken from his home and forced to open the doors, when the guards were disarmed and shut up in the guard house.

It was believed in Hunnewell, Kansas, yesterday that Danford, the broken bank president, would probably be lynched before this morning. A committee appointed by the unfortunate depositors to go to Wichita and investigate the value of the collaterals "abstracted" from Danford's Caldwell bank, has returned to Hunnewell and reported that not more than 20 cents on the dollar can be paid. The mob having Danford in charge was on the lookout yesterday for the arrival of militia to protect the prisoners
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A2:
JACKSON, OHIO, THURSDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1881.
Another Murder Near Ironton.
The good people of Ironton have been considerably excited on account of a murder just east of the city limits. Dr. Joseph A. Beggs was clerk at Etna Iron Works, and an eminent chemist. He was shot and killed near eleven o'clock at night, by Bill Zeck and John Wagoner. We have carefully read the testimony taken at the Coroner's inquest, as reported in the Ironton papers, and there appears to be considerable mystery about it. The case appears to be mixed up with bad women, beer and tobacco. The murderers, and the persons who were present, testify that a man came to Wagoner's house and commenced whistling and kicking against the fence. He was asked what he wanted, and what his name was. He said his name was "Old Hell." When he would not go away they shot him. There is other evidence, tending to show that the murder was committed at a point on the railroad, and not at Wagoner's house.

The citizens of Ironton have held a meeting, and passed resolutions requesting Judge Harper to hold a special term of Court to try the murderers. They also appointed a committee to raise money for the widow and children of the murdered man.

The Ironton papers speak of Dr. Beggs as a quiet, inoffensive, moral, good citizen. People sometimes differ on these questions. In Ironton, it seems, a man may spend his time and money at a beer hell until near midnight, smoking cigars and swilling beer, and yet be a model of morality in that moral city. Fanatics, like ourself, view it in a different light. In order to explain our meaning, we publish part of the testimony of two or three of the witnesses:

Jesse W. Maynard.—Myself. Cyrus Palmer and Lafayette Mead were going home from Ironton about 10 and 11 o'clock and stopped at Lion Garden to get a drink just before and the saloon keeper were sitting there reading and smoking. We went out again, and Palmer and I stood and talked 15 or 20 minutes, and sitting on Beggs came out of the saloon and walked just in and turned off the path to the right just by the Le Page house. We kept on up the plike, and about the third telegraph post above elm tree house heard some one say, "there goes the dragon and a cigar, and in the air on a keeper heard a gun fire, and in a short time heard another shot; thought a little further down and a fainter pistol.

Henry Fisher, proprietor of Lion Garden, and his son, also testified. Mr. Beggs came into the saloon about 8 or 9. In a short time, Palmer and his partners came in, got a glass of beer each, and went out. Beggs carried a cigar, and took a glass of beer there. When the three men went out, he was the only customer left, and he remained quite a time with Mr. Fisher. He had taken another beer at the bar, and finally took another beer at the bar. He passed out a little before ten, the Fishers thought, and was seen by them for a few steps, going up the road.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A5:
ONLY TWO HANGINGS.
Anderson Jones Pays the Penalty Under the Forms of Law, But Ohio Lynchers Attend to John Wagner.
John Wagoner Lynched.

IRONTON, O., Jan. 20.—John Wagoner, one of the murderers of Dr. Joseph Biggs, who was shot after night on a lonesome path near the Etna Iron works nearly two months ago, was taken from the county jail by a well-organized band last night, and hanged in the court house yard. One of his accomplices, Wm. Zeck, was also taken out, and with the rope around his neck made a confession that there was an organized band in the vicinity for murder and robbery. Dr. Beggs was killed for his money, but they only got one silver dollar. He said Biggs was either killed by Sarah Zeck, John Wagoner or Frank Marshall. He says he himself was in the house at the time Mrs. Wagoner, mother of John, told them to tie a bar of pig iron to Beggs' neck and sink the body in the river, but then concluded to try a different plan, and carried the body where it was found, and then went after the officers and told them they had killed him in self defense; but the people were morally certain, from the glaring improbabilities embodied in the history, that Beggs had been murdered. The developments of last night have proved that this opinion was correct. After his confession Zeck was returned to the jail. Wagoner refused to say anything, and was strung up to a tree.

Augusta, Ga., Jan. 20. — Anderson Johns, colored, was hanged privately to-day in the jail yard, for the murder of John S. Haroldson, on December 9, 1881,. He made no confession.

Cincinnati, Jan. 20. — The Times-Star Ironton special says; John Wagoner, one of the murderers of Dr. Biggs, who was killed two months ago, was taken out of the jail between 12 and 1 o'clock last night and hung in the court house yard, by a party of from forty to sixty masked men. They first took Bill Zeek, the other accused murderer, whereupon he confessed, implicating others, who have not yet been arrested, and the let him live for the present. They then departed in wagons. There is not a trace or clue to the perpetrators, and public opinion apparently approves the act.

Augusta, Ga., Jan. 20. — Jones, who was hanged to-day made a confession that he killed Horraldson in his store with an axe, and then stole $42 from him. Jones dropped into poetry while in the jail.

A Newark, N. J., dispatch says that James B. Graves, who shot E. P. Sodon, pleaded "irresistable impulse."
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A11:
When a man is hung by a mob in Ohio they break the news gently. One John Wagoner was lynched at Ironton, Ohio, last Friday night, as mentioned in our dispatches the next day. A special to the Cincinnati Commercial, givse a long account of the affair, from which the following sentences are culled:

Last night for the first time in the history of Lawrence county, the slow process of the law was dispensed with, and speedy, inflexible justice administered to one murderer at least. Your readers are by this time all familiar with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, last November, an event which at the time filled this community with horror. Directly after the murder there were many threats of lynching. So many murders had been committed within the last few years in this country, and so many murderers, through the stupidity and rascality of jurors, gone unhanged, that the community and the best citizens were almost desperate. Things seemed to have reached a most dangerous state, and it was the general opinion that something radical would have to soon be done. This feeling threatened a long rope and a short shrift to the murderers.

Everything so far had been done with the regularity of macinery, and with absolutely no noise, confusion or outery. It was no mob made of the rabble got together in the excitement of the moment, that was doing these things. There were not more than forty or fifty in the band. All were masked. Each had his number. There was not only a leader, but also Captains of squads. All orders were given to the numbers, it was "No. 9 here." The commands were in a low and disguised tone. Everything evinced careful drill by intelligent men.

Lynch law in any but unorganized communities is a most dangerous and destructive thing. We trust, however, that if good results can possibly flow from its exercise, this terrible affair will have its lasting lesson. It may possibly strike terror into the hearts of an element that too little fears justice as administered in our courts.

As soon the guards over them were removed the mob dispersed, no one knows whither. Not a soul, so far as is known, recognized anyone of the band of lynchers. They were effectively disguised.

And all this in the glorious climate of Ohio. The only remark made by the Commercial editorially is this: "The hanging of John Wagoner by an organized body of masked men is but the prelude of what is coming if the law is not more efficiently and sternly administered in this country." This man no doubt, deserved hanging, but the mob had no more right
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A15:
LAST Friday did not furnish the usual nota of hangings. A negro murderer
LAST Friday did not furnish the usual quota of hangings. A negro murderer was hung in Georgia; but at Ironton, O., the murderer of Dr. Byers, paymaster of a furnace, was lynched, being taken from jail and hung in the Court House Yard. This is the second case in Ohio within a short time, the other having been in the neighboring county of Athens. Of course this lynching is all wrong as long as the law may operate, and surely, in Ohio, there is no occasion for lynching.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A16:
More Lynch Law.
Our readers will remember that several weeks ago we mentioned the murder of Dr. Beggs, near Ironton. He was shot as he was going home from a saloon, about eleven o'clock at night. A man named Zeek, and another named Waggoner, were arrested and sent to jail. Zeek has made a confession, and says that Waggoner, who is his brother-in-law, did the shooting.

On just Thursday night a mob of disguised men took Waggoner out of the jail and hung him on a tree, near the Court House.

We believe, the way the criminal law is now not being administered, that this was right. In order to make lynch law a terror to evil-doers, it must extend, in some cases, to Judges and jurors.

A short time ago the Ironton Bee had an editorial in favor of abolishing juries, and among other sensible things said:

Our own county is a sad illustration of the evils of the jury system. We are over $13,000 in debt on our expense fund alone, because juries have failed both of defendants who infested the immediate vicinity of Hanging Rock, when at last brought into Court, escaped through the Jury. One languishes in the penitentiary. But not because he committed the bonest acts on the calendar. The Jury absorbed that, because one of the members didn't want to "dissagree the family." But the criminal unwittingly plead guilty to perjury, and the judge (most noble Judge I) gave him the shortest sentence the law allowed.

The county bears the expense of these useless prosecutions. The Jury says in effect to the criminal, "Well done!" and to his associates, "Go thou, and do likewise."

It is no safety for life or property, no protection or satisfaction in law. Ignorant men make the best jurors, and ignorant men are the most bigoted and obstinate. There are many bad features in our laws which need to be remedied, but the worst of them all is the criminal jury.

Between Judge Lynch and the modern jury, with its ineptible sprinkling of "smart alcoaks" and obstinate ignoramuses, we are decidedly of the opinion, the former would be much more speedy and effectual than the latter.
Between Judge Lynch and the modern jury, with its ineptly sprinkling of "smart alceks" and obstinate ignoramuses, we are decidedly of the opinion, the former would be much more speedy and effectual in the suppression of crime. The people will be compelled to take the law, their own hands, and our opinion is to do it, the better, if these outbreaking crimes continue.

Self-protection is the first law of nature, and when it has been fully demonstrated that the law is incapable of protecting them, it is time tozeno project himself and his family. If it becomes necessary to drive out the whole set of soundrels from whom these outrages emanate, let the citizens organize and do it thoroughly. In other words, let us have peace and order, if we have to fight for it.

And to our Legislators let us say: "Away with the Jury!"

Mob Law in Ohio.

Mob Law in Ohio.

John Wagoner, in jail at Ironton, Lawrence County, Ohio, charged with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, of that place, last November, was taken from jail by fifty masked men on the night of January 19 and hanged to a tree in the court-house yard. The crime of which Wagoner was guilty was a very atrocious and unprovoked one, and was committed, it has been thought, for the purpose of robbery. Dr. Beggs was a bookkeeper for an iron company, and was assaulted and murdered while on his way home from the mill, after dark had set in. Wagoner and a man named Zeek, toward whom suspicion so strongly pointed that there was little doubt remained as to their guilt, were arrested charged with the crime. On the night in question, few minutes after 12 o'clock, a knock was heard at the jail, and the Sheriff responded by opening the door. He was seized, overpowered and with cocked revolvers the mob demanded the keys of the jail. The Sheriff firmly refused, and seeing that he would not yield, he was taken into the room of his wife where the demand was repeated in a similar manner. His wife, frightened almost out of her senses, surrendered the keys, and in a moment the door to the cell in which Wagoner and Zeek were confined was swung open and the prisoners were led trembling from the cell. "I didn't mean to kill him," protested Wagoner in a tone of agony, but his words were unheeded and he was hurried into the yard and hanged without any ado. Zeek was so thoroughly frightened that he was scarcely able to stand and was terrorized into a confession. Zeek thought his time had come, and with a countenance ashy pale, related the circumstances of the killing as best he could. His confession was to the effect that he was an accomplice, and that Wagoner did the killing. After Beggs had been struck down, Mrs. Zeek (Zeek's wife) and a Mrs. Hall carried the body of the dead man from the scene to where it was afterward found. After Zeek's confession he was returned to his cell and locked up, evidently the mob desiring to keep him for further testimony respecting those whom he implicated. What Wagoner had to say in his last moments is not known. It is sufficient to know that in two minutes after he was taken from the jail he was suspended by the neck under a tree only a few feet from the court-house. The mob was very orderly in their work, being headed by a leader and all answering promptly to their numbers, showing that they had all been well drilled for the job in advance. Several belated citizens who hap-
their work, being headed by a leader and all answering promptly to their numbers, showing that they had all been well drilled for the job in advance. Several belated citizens who happened to pass while the mob were carrying out their work, were halted by the guards stationed about and kept prisoners until the work was completed. The mob then quietly dispersed, going in all directions. The body of Wagoner was allowed to hang until morning when it was viewed and cut down by the Coroner and handed over to an undertaker. Wagoner was said to be a rather good looking fellow, with mild blue eyes, aquiline nose, mustache and a well shaped face. His features bore no evidence of hanging. Mrs. Hall and Mrs. Zeek were arrested in the morning on the strength of Zeek's confession, but at the time of their arrest they had no knowledge of Wagoner's fate, or Zeek's confession, and asserted their innocence and entire willingness to go with the officers.
